facts.statement: Eocarcharia lived in the western Ténéré Desert of Niger.
facts.quote: Eocarcharia () is an extinct genus of theropod dinosaurs found in what is now the western Ténéré Desert of Niger.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia fossils date to the Early Cretaceous (Aptian–Albian ages) and were found in the Elrhaz Formation at the Gadoufaoua locality.
facts.quote: It is known from several skull bones collected in 2000 by an expedition to the Early Cretaceous (Aptian–Albian ages) Elrhaz Formation (Gadoufaoua locality) led by American paleontologist Paul Sereno.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia was formally described in 2008 by Paul Sereno and Steve Brusatte.
facts.quote: The fossil material was then described in 2008 by Sereno and Steve Brusatte.

facts.statement: The genus Eocarcharia contains only one species, Eocarcharia dinops.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Eocarcharia dinops.

facts.statement: Later studies suggest Eocarcharia may be a chimaera, combining bones from at least two unrelated taxa rather than a single species.
facts.quote: While Sereno and Brusatte identified all of the remains as belonging to a new carcharodontosaurid, later studies suggested that the species is chimaeric, comprising bones of at least two unrelated taxa.

facts.statement: Some researchers propose that the holotype specimen belongs to a baryonychine spinosaurid closely related to Suchomimus.
facts.quote: Some of the Eocarcharia material, including the holotype (name-bearing) specimen, likely belongs to a baryonychine spinosaurid. This would render Eocarcharia a member of this group, closely related to the coeval Suchomimus.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia is characterized by a robust postorbital bone with a large brow.
facts.quote: The postorbital (bone behind the orbit) is robust with a large brow, a distinct characteristic of Eocarcharia.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that Eocarcharia's robust brow was covered in keratin and used for head-butting.
facts.quote: It was possibly covered in keratin and used for head-butting with other individuals of its species.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia inhabited an environment of rivers and vast floodplains shared with other dinosaurs, pterosaurs, and crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: Eocarcharia lived in an environment with rivers and vast floodplains alongside many other dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodylomorphs, and freshwater animals.

facts.statement: When classified as a carcharodontosaurid, Eocarcharia is estimated to have been 6 to 8 meters long.
facts.quote: When considered a carcharodontosaurid, it was estimated to be 6 - 8 m long, making it smaller than derived carcharodontosaurids like Giganotosaurus, and Carcharodontosaurus.

facts.statement: The name Eocarcharia combines Greek words for 'dawn' and 'shark' to reflect its early divergence from 'shark-toothed' relatives.
facts.quote: The generic name, Eocarcharia, derives from the Ancient Greek words eos, meaning dawn, and karcharias, meaning shark, referencing the early-diverging nature of Eocarcharia in relation to its 'shark-toothed' relatives.

facts.statement: The species name dinops means 'fierce-eyed' and refers to the unique ornamentation on the postorbital bone above the eye.
facts.quote: The specific name, dinops, is a Greek term meaning fierce-eyed, referring to the unique postorbital ornamentation above the eye.

facts.statement: The fossil collection includes a maxilla, maxilla fragments, five postorbitals, two frontals, and five teeth.
facts.quote: During the expedition, several isolated theropod skull bones were collected, including a maxilla (main tooth-bearing bone of the upper jaw) and two maxilla fragments, five postorbitals (bone behind the orbit), two frontals—one articulated with the left prefrontal and one with a partial parietal (skull roof bones)—and five teeth.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Eocarcharia is the postorbital bone cataloged as MNN-GAD2.
facts.quote: They established one of the postorbitals, MNN-GAD2, as the holotype (name-bearing) specimen.

facts.statement: The fused skull bones indicate that the referred specimens were fully mature adults.
facts.quote: Based on the total fusion of the skull bones referred to Eocarcharia, Sereno & Brusatte identified them as having come from fully mature adult individuals.

facts.statement: The position of the orbital boss above the top back edge of the orbit is a diagnostic trait unique to Eocarcharia.
facts.quote: This orbital boss is positioned above the posterodorsal (top back) edge of the orbit, a trait noted by Sereno and Brusatte to be diagnostic (unique) to this species.

facts.statement: Unlike Mapusaurus and Giganotosaurus, the postorbital bosses of Eocarcharia lack extensive ossification.
facts.quote: In contrast, the postorbital bosses of Carcharodontosaurus and Eocarcharia lack the extensive ossification seen in Mapusaurus and Giganotosaurus.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia has a narrow postorbital facet articulating with the jugal, distinguishing it from the broader facets of Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Another diagnostic trait of Eocarcharia is that its postorbital bears a narrow facet which articulates laterally with the jugal (cheekbone), whereas carcharodontosaurids like Carcharodontosaurus have broader facets.

facts.statement: The midshaft of the ventral ramus of the Eocarcharia postorbital is subtriangular in cross-section, unlike the U-shape found in spinosaurids and megalosaurids.
facts.quote: Midshafts of the ventral (bottom) ramus (a branch of bone) of the postorbital in spinosaurids and megalosaurids are typically U-shaped in cross-section, whereas in Eocarcharia it is subtriangular in cross-section.

facts.statement: The prefrontal bone in Eocarcharia is relatively wide, approximately half the width of the frontal bone.
facts.quote: In Eocarcharia, the prefrontal is relatively wide, about half the width of the frontal.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia retains unfused independent prefrontals, a trait shared with earlier genera but absent in advanced carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Independent prefrontals are absent in advanced carcharodontosaurids as they are typically co-ossified (fused) with the lacrimals into a single element, whereas in earlier genera like Eocarcharia, Acrocanthosaurus, and Concavenator, they are unfused.

facts.statement: The dentary bone of the Eocarcharia taxon possesses 15 tooth sockets.
facts.quote: The dentary has 15 alveoli (tooth sockets).

facts.statement: The teeth of the Eocarcharia taxon have transversely compressed crowns.
facts.quote: The tooth crowns are transversely compressed.

facts.statement: Teeth referred to Eocarcharia are not blade-shaped and lack the straight posterior carina and high-relief enamel wrinkles common in other carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Unlike many carcharodontosaurid teeth, those referred to Eocarcharia are not blade-shaped and they lack straight posterior carina (cutting edges on the back of the crown) and enamel wrinkles with high relief.

facts.statement: Initially, all referred material was classified as a single species of early-diverging carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: All of the material was initially recognized as belonging to the same species, specifically an early-diverging carcharodontosaurid.

facts.statement: Sereno and Brusatte described Eocarcharia in 2008 as an early-diverging allosauroid theropod within the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Sereno & Brusatte (2008) recognized Eocarcharia as an allosauroid theropod in an early-diverging position within the family Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.statement: Sereno and Brusatte named the genus Kryptops palaios in their 2008 paper describing Eocarcharia.
facts.quote: In the same 2008 paper, Sereno and Brusatte named Kryptops palaios based on an abelisaurid maxilla and postcranial remains.

facts.statement: Matthew Carrano and colleagues hypothesized in 2012 that the holotype of Kryptops palaios was a chimera containing postcranial bones possibly belonging to Eocarcharia.
facts.quote: In 2012, Matthew Carrano and colleagues considered Kryptops palaios to be a chimera (specimen composed of multiple species), stating that its postcranial remains, especially the pelvis and sacrum, may belong to a carcharodontosaurid, possibly Eocarcharia.

facts.statement: Cau and Paterna noted that two unique traits proposed for Eocarcharia are also shared with the spinosaurid Ceratosuchops.
facts.quote: Cau and Paterna further recognized that two of the autapomorphies (unique derived traits) proposed for Eocarcharia by Sereno and Brusatte are also uniquely shared with Ceratosuchops, a baryonychine from the Wessex Formation of the United Kingdom.

facts.statement: Cau and Paterna considered Eocarcharia to be a spinosaurid based on its similarities to Suchomimus, Ceratosuchops, and Riparovenator.
facts.quote: Given the discrepancies with the placement of Eocarcharia as a carcharodontosaur and the many similarities to Suchomimus, Ceratosuchops, and Riparovenator, the researchers considered the genus to be most parsimoniously regarded as a spinosaurid.

facts.statement: Cau and Paterna placed Eocarcharia as the sister taxon to the spinosaurid Suchomimus in their phylogenetic analysis.
facts.quote: Cau and Paterna's phylogenetic results placed Eocarcharia as the sister taxon to Suchomimus.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that the brow of Eocarcharia was covered in keratin, which would have extended its size.
facts.quote: The brow was likely covered in keratin, extending its size.

facts.statement: Sereno and Brusatte hypothesized that the postorbital bosses of Eocarcharia were used for intraspecific lateral head-butting.
facts.quote: This led the authors to hypothesize that the postorbital brows of Eocarcharia and carcharodontosaurids were used for intraspecific lateral head-butting.

facts.statement: Fossils of Eocarcharia have been found in the Elrhaz Formation of the Tegama Group in the Gadoufaoua area of the Nigerian Ténéré Desert.
facts.quote: Eocarcharia is known from the Elrhaz Formation of the Tegama Group in an area of the Nigerian Ténéré Desert called Gadoufaoua.

facts.statement: Eocarcharia likely inhabited habitats dominated by inland floodplains or riparian zones.
facts.quote: It likely lived in habitats dominated by inland floodplains (a riparian zone).

facts.statement: Eocarcharia coexisted with theropods including the spinosaurid Suchomimus, the chimeric Kryptops, and the noasaurid Afromimus.
facts.quote: Eocarcharia lived alongside several other dinosaurs. These included other theropods, such as the spinosaurid and probable close relative Suchomimus, Kryptops (known from a chimaeric combination of abelisaurid and allosauroid material), and the putative noasaurid Afromimus.

facts.statement: The fossil site of Gadoufaoua contains remains of megaherbivores such as Ouranosaurus, Lurdusaurus, Elrhazosaurus, Nigersaurus, and an unnamed titanosaur.
facts.quote: Several megaherbivores, including the hadrosauriforms Ouranosaurus and Lurdusaurus, the dryosaurid Elrhazosaurus, and two sauropods, the rebbachisaurid Nigersaurus and an unnamed titanosaur, have been unearthed from Gadoufaoua.

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Eocarcharia as Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Carcharodontosauridae

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Eocarcharia is Eocarcharia dinops.
facts.quote: Type species: Eocarcharia dinops

facts.statement: The time range for Eocarcharia is recorded as 121.4 to 100.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (121.4 to 100.5 million years ago)

rejected.quote: While the maxilla and teeth clearly belong to a carcharodontosaurid or similar taxon, later research has suggested the holotype and skull roof may belong to an unrelated theropod, specifically a spinosaurid closely related to Suchomimus.
